Carbon Dioxide (CO2-C) flux
methodology:
Carbon dioxide gas fluxes were calculated from change in gas concentration over time using best fit linear model. Two methods were used for measuring gas fluxes: 1. gas chromatography (GC) and 2. photoacoustic infrared spectroscopy (PAS). 1. For GC gas measurements, we followed the methods described in Gracenet protocol (http://www.ars.usda.gov/research/programs/programs.htm?np_code=212&docid=21223&page=2; Ch. 3). Gas sampling points to calculate gas flux were variable (3-4) across sites. However, at least three gas sampling points were used to ensure accurate gas flux calculation. Gas chamber size and volume varied across the sites, and were included in the gas flux equation to adjust for accurate gas flux calculation. 2. For PAS gas measurements, we followed the protocol described in Adviento-Borbe dissertation (http://www.ars.usda.gov/research/programs/programs.htm?np_code=212&docid=21223&page=2; Ch. 2). The PAS gas measurements were compared to conventional GC measurements and found gas fluxes from PAS and GC are comparable (Iqbal et al., 2013).
Note that the acceptable value range is based on final gas flux values. For "on_and_off_fert_band" the row gas flux values correspond to the final values. For "on_broadcast" measurements the final values can be calculated by taking a simple average (if there is more than one measurement), while a weighted average should be used for "on_fert_band" and "off_fert_band" measurements (for example: 20% on_fert_band + 80% off_fert_band).

short_description: Carbon Dioxide (CO2) coefficient of determination (R2)

methodology:

short_description: Method used for measuring GHG fluxes with PAS = photoacoustic infrared spectroscopy, GC = gas chromatography
methodology: Greenhouse gas fluxes were measured by static chambers deployed on the soil surface for a period of typically no more than 60 min. During chamber deployment, gas samples were collected at regular intervals and analyzed using photoacoustic infrared spectroscopy (PAS) or gas chromatography (GC). Some sites used both across years.

short_description: Chamber position
methodology: Chamber positions are assigned for each plot where GHG chambers were placed to get representative gas fluxes. Chambers were positioned with respect to fertilizer placement because a chamber placed on or off of the fertilized area could make a significant difference in GHG emissions. The "band" is the application of N fertilizer usually in the form of urea ammonium nitrate solution injected in bands up to to 15 cm soil depth. Specifically, "on_fert_band" means the chamber was placed over the fertilizer band, and "off_fert_band" means the chamber was placed where no fertilizer was applied. Some chambers were positioned to be over the banded area and the non-fertilized area, these are labeled "on_and_off_fert_band". Experiments that received a uniform, broadcast application of fertilizer are labeled as "on broadcast".

short_description: Insect population
units: Activity-Density (for Pitfall Traps), Abundance / 15 pendulum sweeps (for Sweep Netting), Average Species / sticky trap / day (for Sticky Traps)
methodology:
Canopy insect or arthropod population was estimated using one of the three sampling method: Pitfall Traps, Sweep Netting, Sticky Traps.

Pitfall traps were used to estimate the activity-density of ground-dwelling arthropods. Three pitfall traps were placed within each sampled plot, and consisted of 1 L cups (Reynolds Food Packaging, Shepherdsville, Kentucky) buried in the ground flush with the soil surface. A cover, raised 5 cm above the soil surface, was used to prevent debris from entering pitfall traps. To prevent arthropods from escaping traps, the bottom of each pitfall container was filled with 100 mL of non-scented, soapy water solution. Pitfall traps were placed in the plots on "Placement Date" and remained in plots for 24 h during each sampling period. After 24 h, contents of pitfall traps were placed separately into sealable plastic bags and stored in freezers until contents were sorted. Insects captured in pitfall traps were identified to family, and non-insect arthropods were identified to class, order, or family depending upon the taxa. Only beneficial arthropods (i.e., predators, detritivores, granivores) were identified. 

Sweep nets were used to sample beneficial arthropods in soybean canopies. A sample consisted of 15 continuous pendulum sweeps of the upper soybean canopy. Sweeping locations within plots were arbitrarily chosen, but never at plot edges. One sweep net sample was collected per plot. Sweep net sample contents were separately placed in sealable plastic bags and stored in freezers until contents were sorted. Insects captured by sweeps nets were identified to family or superfamily, and non-insect arthropods were identified to order. 

Adult rootworm, bean leaf beetle and lady beetles were sampled from plots with unbaited Pherocon AM yellow sticky traps (referred to as sticky traps; Trece Inc., Adair, OK). Three sticky traps were placed within each plot. Sticky traps were attached to corn plants at ear height in corn plots and were affixed to poles above the top of the canopy in soybean and wheat plots. Traps remained in plots for roughly 1 week. The total number adult rootworm, bean leaf beetle and lady beetles captured by each sticky trap were counted and then averaged per plot.

short_description: Position assessed for damage or disease
Visual rating of damage due to disease or insect
methodology:
Stalk Rot Rating
Pushed 5-15 consecutive stalks, depending on plot size, roughly 30 degrees and recorded if the stalk lodged (yes/no). Data represent the number of lodged plants out of total measured per plot.  

Corn Ear Rot Rating
Rated 5-15 consecutive ears, depending on plot size, by pulling back the husk and estimating disease severity as a percentage of ear rot in relation to the total ear. Incidence and severity for each ear were recorded separately prior to harvest.

Corn Foliar Disease Rating
Assessed foliar disease severity of the ear leaf and the leaf +2 from the ear on 10 consecutive plants. Disease severity was assessed as a percentage of total lesion area for each foliar disease present on each leaf at R5.5 (dent stage). 

Soybean Stem Disease Rating
For each plot, estimated the severity of stem diseases.

Soybean Foliar Disease Rating
In three rows per plot, assessed foliar disease severity on 10 consecutive plants. Ten leaves in the upper and 10 leaves in the lower canopy were assessed for disease severity. For leaves in the lower canopy, estimated which node the leaves were on, and tried to consistently assess leaves from similar nodes. Disease severity was assessed as a percentage of total leaf area affected for each terminal leaflet at R6 (full seed).

short_description: Soil sampling depth
methodology: Soil measurements were collected primarily in depths of 0-10, 10-20, 20-40, and 40-60 cm. Soil nitrate was the common exception as it was 0-30, 30-60, and 60-90 cm.

short_description: Bulk density
methodology: Soil dry bulk density was to be determined in spring when soil is moist and clays are still fully hydrated after winter rewetting. It could be before planting or within a month after planting and soil settling after several rainfalls. Samples were to be taken in the quarter-row position at four depths: 0 to 10 cm (0 to 3.9 in), 10 to 20 cm (3.9 to 7.9 in), 20 to 40 cm (7.9 to 15.7 in), and 40 to 60 cm (15.7 to 23.6 in). Hand core samples were to be used for the top two depths, while the deeper two depths could use either hand cores or hydraulic probe cores. A minimum of three replicate cores per depth per plot were to be collected at least in years one, three, and five. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Water retention at 0 bar
methodology: Water retention curves were measured on the intact cores (see bulk density for sampling details) for a series of steps including 0 (saturated), -0.05, -0.10, -0.33, and -15 bar, with additional freely drained for surface samples for greenhouse gas studies. Bulk density samples could be used for the saturated, freely drained, -0.05, -0.10, and -0.33 bar. The wilting point (-15 bar) was to be determined on < 2 mm (0.08 in) crush soil. It was required to measure water retention curves on 0 to 10 cm (0 to 3.9 in) and 10 to 20 cm (3.9 to 7.9 in) depths, but was highly encouraged to measure at all four depths in years one, three, and five. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Infiltration rate
methodology: Infiltration rate was to be determined using the double-ring method. A constant head of water was kept in center ring for three hours, and then covered with plastic. Twenty-four (24) hours later soil samples were taken with depth in the center ring, for measure of redistributed water and a field estimate of field capacity. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Soil texture name
methodology: Soil texture was to be measured on every plot, once at the beginning of the study using the hydrometer method. Samples were to be taken at four depths: 0 to 10 cm (0 to 3.9 in), 10 to 20 cm (3.9 to 7.9 in), 20 to 40 cm (7.9 to 15.7 in), and 40 to 60 cm (15.7 to 23.6 in). For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Aggregate stability
methodology: Aggregate stability was to be determined by wet-sieving method (using Yoder type wet-sieving apparatus). Soil samples were to be taken while soil was moist and friable, then gently pushed through 8 mm screen and air-dried. If samples were not to be run within 4 to 6 weeks of drying, they should be kept in cold room until analysis. Mean weight diameter (MWD) and water stable aggregates were calculated to express/quantify aggregate stability. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Soil pH
methodology: Soil pH was to be measured with a standard 1:1 soil:water ratio in years one, three, and five. A minimum of 12 push-probe samples composited into one bag per plot and depth, or a minimum of 3 samples composited from bulk density cores (see bulk density for sampling details). Samples were to be air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm (0.08 in) sieve before sent for analysis. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Cation exchange capacity (CEC)
methodology: Cation exchange capacity (CEC) was to be determined in years one, three, and five using the standard commercial lab procedure of estimating by summing major cations plus hydrogen (H) from buffer pH. However, for soil sample depths with free carbonates, the more expensive analysis was suggested to be done. A minimum of 12 push-probe samples composited into one bag per plot and depth, or a minimum of 3 samples composited from bulk density cores (see bulk density for sampling details). Samples were to be air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm (0.08 in) sieve before sent for analysis. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

short_description: Soil organic carbon (SOC)
methodology: Soil organic carbon (SOC) was to be determined by dry combustion after checking for calcareous conditions and accounting for inorganic C on samples from all four depths in years one, three, and five. A minimum of 12 push-probe samples composited into one bag per plot and depth, or a minimum of 3 samples composited from bulk density cores (see bulk density for sampling details). Samples were to be air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm (0.08 in) sieve. Subsamples of the <2 mm (0.08 in) fraction were to be ball milled or finely ground to pass a 250 m sieve for C analysis. For further details refer to Kladivko et al. (2014), Standardized research protocols enable transdisciplinary research of climate variation impacts in corn production systems. Journal of Soil Water Conservation, 69 (6):532-542, http://dx.doi.org/10.2489/jswc.69.6.532.

Samples were to be air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm (0.08 in) sieve. Subsamples of the <2 mm (0.08 in) fraction were to be ball milled or finely ground to pass a 250 m sieve for N analysis. Tile nitrate-N concentration
methodology: Drainage water Nitrate-N concentration was determined on samples collected from the control structure (or sump) using automatic water sampler. Where or when the sampling system was not available, grab samples were collected on regular (weekly or biweekly) base. Water samples were stored in a refrigerator at 4deg C or frozen until analyzed, generally for a couple weeks to a month. Before chemical analysis each sample was well-mixed and then filtered through a glass fiber.
